newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: COCOA--Amsterdam gears up to receive more in bulk.
newsitem.headline: COCOA--Amsterdam gears up to receive more in bulk.

text.p: Amsterdam port is gearing up for more cocoa in the current season and sees a trend towards bulk shipment as the key to keeping up its position as the world's premier cocoa port, industry sources said on Friday.
The port has applied to the city council for a grant of 7.7 million guilders to build its first warehouse specifically designed to handle bulk and is confident of receiving the funds.

"The promotion of bulk cocoa is the future and these warehouses are absolutely necessary to keep Amsterdam as the leading cocoa port in the world," Louis Bensdorp, president of the Dutch Cocoa Association (NCV) told Reuters.
Bensdorp said the amount of cocoa processed in the Netherlands is expected to increase to around 400,000 tonnes in the 1996/1997 (Oct-Sept) season, up from 385,000 last season.
He estimated that between 200,000 and 250,000 tonnes of cocoa would arrive as bulk shipment, more than double the amount imported as such last season.

Amsterdam port officials said the council grant would finance the construction of a multi-purpose warehouse complex which would be capable of storing between 50,000 and 60,000 tonnes of cocoa in bulk.
The port plans to lease the facility to stevedoring company Ter Haak under a long-term contract and said the project carries no financial risk for the port.
A final decision on the grant is expected in the next few days but a port spokesman said he was confident the go-ahead would be given.

Amsterdam currently handles around 500,000 tonnes of cocoa every year and although there were some bulk shipments last season, these either went straight through to industry customers or were kept in modified warehouses.
"The new bulk warehouse has to be next to the water with a conveyor belt to get the cocoa in," the port's project manager Remco Barkhuis said.
The warehouse is also higher than normal as bulk cocoa can be stored to a height of around nine or ten metres, with specially-constructed internal partition walls for stability.
"These walls will be removable to allow other products to be stored outside of the cocoa season," Barkhuis said.
There were other modifications such as special temperature, moisture and lighting controls, he added.
Industry sources said the increase in the Dutch cocoa grind reflected strong output at the country's main processors but also a likely small dip at one in particular.
"The main grinders will be processing slightly more beans but one company, Bensdorp Cocoa, will switch to using more liquor, imported from the Ivory Coast," one said.
A spokesman at Bensdorp, confirmed that the company would be processing more cocoa liquor, describing it as a "logistical exercise" but said the changes would be very minimal.
Industry sources said the trend towards European companies importing liquor, processed from beans locally in the Ivory Coast, was one that was expected to continue.
The Ivory Coast has said it want to process an increasing amount of cocoa in local factories.
